tldr: To address the issue where small joint position tracking errors still result in a loss of expressive nuance and dynamics, the authors propose a residual learning framework that explicitly compensates for amplitude, energy, body expansion, and other motion characteristics, achieving highly expressive reproduction on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid robot.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed residual compensation framework. Reference motions are segmented into motion units, and motion-specific residual policies are trained on top of a frozen whole-body tracker and distilled into a single unified residual policy with motion-aware gating for adaptive compensation.
overview:
For humanoid robots to convey emotions and intentions like humans, it is not enough to simply trace target joint positions. They must also faithfully reproduce expressive qualities such as the amplitude of a hand wave or the dynamics of a gesture. However, existing reinforcement learning-based whole-body tracking controllers prioritize maintaining balance to prevent falls and minimizing average position tracking errors across the body. As a result, critical expressive characteristics—like the depth of a bow or the energetic momentum of a wave—tend to be attenuated.

Based on the insight that lower average positional tracking error does not guarantee better preservation of dynamic and postural motion characteristics, the authors propose a residual learning framework that restores expressiveness while keeping existing trackers frozen. Specifically, they define five expressive motion descriptors: amplitude, kinetic energy, body expansion, body lean, and pelvis height. A residual policy is trained with reward objectives targeting these values. In addition, they introduce "motion-aware gating," which provides larger correction capacity to actively moving parts while suppressing unnecessary disturbance in parts that should remain still.

Experiments in simulation and on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid across eight motion categories demonstrate that the proposed method preserves tracking stability while achieving faithful reproduction across all five motion descriptors compared to baselines.
contributions: Experimentally demonstrated that simply minimizing average positional tracking error is insufficient to preserve the dynamic and postural characteristics of motions.
Proposed a residual learning framework for frozen trackers that directly compensates for motion amplitude, kinetic energy, body expansion, body lean, and pelvis height.

Introduced a motion-aware gating mechanism that dynamically allocates correction capacity based on body-part activity, balancing the recovery of primary motion expressiveness with the stability of supporting parts.

Distilled category-specific teacher policies into a single unified policy and demonstrated superior expressive preservation across eight motion categories, including real-world tests on the Unitree G1.

sections.heading: Why Tracking Joint Positions Alone Fails to Convey Expressiveness
sections.summary: When humanoids reproduce expressive gestures, heavily prioritizing fall prevention often sacrifices the vigor of the motion and the depth of the posture. This paper proposes a residual learning approach that restores expressive characteristics while keeping an existing tracker frozen.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to convey intentions and emotions through a physical body, coordinated whole-body movement is essential. Actions possess intrinsic expressive hallmarks, such as the amplitude of the hand during a greeting wave or the forward trunk inclination during a bow.

In recent years, advances in deep reinforcement learning-based whole-body controllers have enabled single policies to track a wide variety of reference motions. However, to maintain balance and prevent falls, robots inevitably deviate from the reference trajectories. Because existing trackers are trained to minimize average keypoint errors across the whole body, local and vital expressive traits—such as large hand gestures or deep forward leans—get washed out. In short, lower average tracking error does not equate to better expressive motion.

To overcome this, the authors turned to residual learning, adding corrections to the outputs of a pre-trained, frozen whole-body tracker. They quantify dynamic characteristics (amplitude, energy) and postural characteristics (body expansion, body lean, pelvis height) and train a residual policy to directly compensate for them. By pairing this with motion-aware gating, which concentrates corrections on actively moving body parts, the method aims to simultaneously maintain physical stability and recover expressive richness.

captions.F2: Overall workflow of the proposed residual compensation framework. It starts with motion unit segmentation, followed by reinforcement learning of motion-specific teacher policies (Stage I), distillation into a single unified student policy (Stage II), and real-world deployment via motion-aware gating (Stage III).

sections.heading: Analyzing Expressive Movement and Adapting Whole-Body Control
sections.summary: The paper outlines prior research on quantifying human emotional expression and motion characteristics, as well as advances in whole-body tracking and residual reinforcement learning, clearly situating this work within the literature.
sections.details:
This research builds upon two main lineages: expressive motion analysis and whole-body tracking & residual adaptation.

### II-A Expressive Motion Analysis
In human behavioral studies and animation, physical traits such as body openness, joint velocities, and trunk tilt are well known to directly convey emotion and intent. Prior work includes Laban Movement Analysis-based studies and emotion recognition using motion energy and geometric features. In virtual avatars, researchers have extracted key poses from gaits to preserve expressiveness. In robotics, methods have been proposed to learn preferred motion styles from human feedback or integrate style transfer into whole-body tracking. Drawing on these insights, this work defines five concrete descriptors that can serve directly as humanoid control objectives.

### II-B Whole-Body Motion Tracking and Residual Adaptation
Reinforcement learning for humanoid whole-body tracking has progressed rapidly, enabling the imitation of diverse behaviors. Furthermore, residual reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective tool for adapting pre-trained controllers to out-of-distribution motions, object manipulation, and sim-to-real dynamics gaps. While most existing residual adaptation approaches target tracking error reduction or task success rates, this work uniquely focuses on explicitly recovering expressive characteristics of posture and motion dynamics.

sections.heading: How the Residual Policy and Motion-Aware Gating Restore Expression
sections.summary: Motions are partitioned into units to compute five expressive descriptors. A unified residual policy is built via reinforcement learning and behavioral cloning distillation, complemented by a gating mechanism that gives active parts wider correction ranges.
sections.details:
The proposed framework consists of data curation, expressive descriptor definition, motion-aware gating, and residual policy training and distillation.

### III-A Problem Formulation
For a base joint position command $\mathbf{a}_t^{\mathrm{wbt}}$ output by a frozen whole-body tracker $\pi_{\mathrm{wbt}}$, a residual policy $\pi_{\mathrm{res}}$ predicts a correction term $\Delta\hat{\mathbf{a}}_t^{\mathrm{res}} \in [-1, 1]^{n_a}$. The final command is $\mathbf{a}_t = \mathbf{a}_t^{\mathrm{wbt}} + \alpha \,\mathbf{g}_t \odot \Delta\hat{\mathbf{a}}_t^{\mathrm{res}}$, where $\alpha = 0.2\,\mathrm{rad}$ (about 11.5 degrees) is the maximum correction scale, $\mathbf{g}_t \in [0.2, 1]^{n_a}$ is the motion-aware gate, and $\odot$ denotes element-wise multiplication.

### III-B Data Curation
Eight categories are selected from the AMASS dataset: walking, kicking, punching, squatting, waving, clapping, crossing arms, and bowing. These are retargeted to the Unitree G1 robot using SOMA. Each motion is split into "motion units" (periodic motion, single action, or static hold), which serve as evaluation intervals for the descriptors.

### III-C Expressive Motion Descriptors
Five expressive descriptors are defined:
- Amplitude: The diameter of trajectories for hands, ankles, and waist in the pelvis-local frame.
- Energy: The sum of squared joint angle differences, acting as a kinematic measure of vigor.
- Body Expansion: The distance from the chest center to both elbows and wrists.
- Body Lean: The sine of the trunk pitch angle in the world frame, $\sin\theta_t$.
- Pelvis Height: The vertical distance from the supporting foot sole to the pelvis.

### III-D Motion-Aware Residual Control
The 29 joints are divided into 5 groups (left/right arms, left/right legs, waist). An activity score $r_{t,b}$ is calculated from the root-mean-square (RMS) velocity of the reference motion over the next 10 steps. The gating $\mathbf{g}_t$ assigns the full correction range ($\pm 0.2\,\mathrm{rad}$) to the most active body part, while retaining a 20% minimum correction range ($\pm 0.04\,\mathrm{rad}$) for less active parts to permit postural adjustments. This concentrates corrections where needed while avoiding unnecessary shaking.

### III-E Residual Policy Training
Policies are trained using PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization). The reward includes an expressive preservation reward $r_{\mathrm{exp}}$, a constraint reward $r_{\mathrm{con}}$ to prevent tracking errors from exploding, and a regularization term $r_{\mathrm{reg}}$ to penalize abrupt changes. Individual teacher policies are trained for each motion category and then distilled into a single unified student policy $\pi_{\mathrm{res}}^{\mathrm{uni}}$ using DAgger.

sections.heading: Validation in Simulation and on the Physical Unitree G1
sections.summary: Evaluated against three baseline trackers (SONIC, GMT, TWIST2), the proposed method significantly reduced errors across all five expressive metrics in both simulation and real-world robot experiments.
sections.details:
Evaluation was performed in simulation (MuJoCo Warp environment) and on a physical humanoid robot (Unitree G1, height 1.32 m, 29 degrees of freedom). Three existing trackers served as baselines: SONIC, GMT, and TWIST2.

### IV-A & IV-B Expressive Preservation and Recovery
A residual model trained simply to minimize position tracking error (Track-Res) reduced positional error (MPKPE), but in several cases worsened trunk lean and energy errors. This clearly confirms that improved positional tracking accuracy does not guarantee better expressiveness.
In contrast, the proposed method (w/ Res.) achieved the lowest error across all five expressive descriptors when combined with each of the three base trackers. For example, pelvis height during deep squats and amplitude and kinetic energy during waving were substantially improved. Motion completion rates without falling remained extremely high: 100% for SONIC, 98.27% for GMT, and 99.89% for TWIST2.

### IV-C Ablation
The authors evaluated the role of motion-aware gating (MAG). Compared to leaving the gate fully open (correction range constant at 1.0), MAG suppressed end-point position error in inactive parts and improved joint position error (MPJPE) from 3.18 cm to 3.10 cm. Compared to a uniform fixed-width gate, MAG reduced amplitude error by 15.8% and low-activity leg/arm error by 18.1%, proving the benefit of focusing corrections where needed.

### IV-D Real-World Robot Experiments
On the physical Unitree G1, a total of 144 trials were conducted using selected trajectories across all motion categories. Measured robot data showed that applying the compensation consistently reduced errors across all five expressive descriptors relative to baselines for all trackers and motions, producing visibly crisper, more natural gestures.

captions.F7: Snapshots of real-world motion execution on the Unitree G1. For each motion, the left shows without compensation, the right shows with compensation, and the blue overlay shows the reference motion. Stepping into punches, kick height, and bow depth show that compensation substantially improves dynamic fidelity to the reference.

sections.heading: Descriptor Coverage and Conflicting Objectives
sections.summary: The authors discuss limitations of the approach, including the inability of five descriptors to capture every nuance and trade-offs where correcting one feature interferes with another.
sections.details:
The method has several limitations:

- Comprehensiveness of expressive descriptors: While amplitude, energy, expansion, lean, and pelvis height are representative metrics, they do not encompass all subtle human nuances. Moreover, because they measure average energy and lean over a motion unit, they can miss transient timing offsets or energy imbalances between different body groups.
- Tracker dependency and conflicting objectives: The system is constrained by the base tracker's characteristics. For instance, in SONIC, the waist range of motion tends to be small, causing the policy to unnaturally move the hips and legs to compensate for trunk forward lean. This negatively affects leg amplitude, kinetic energy, and pelvis height, introducing a trade-off where improving one characteristic degrades another.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Moving Toward More Expressive Humanoid Whole-Body Control
sections.summary: By shifting focus from positional tracking error minimization to expressive feature preservation, this residual learning framework proves its effectiveness in both simulation and real-world humanoid deployment.
sections.details:
This paper presented a residual learning framework with motion-aware gating designed to let humanoid robots fully express intentions and movement nuances.

By establishing dynamic and postural characteristics (amplitude, energy, body expansion, lean, pelvis height) as explicit compensation targets, the method elevates expressive quality without compromising the capabilities of underlying frozen trackers. Extensive experiments in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 robot demonstrate that humanoid expressive capability can be substantially enhanced beyond the pursuit of pure positional tracking accuracy.

takeaways: Low joint position tracking error (such as MPKPE) does not guarantee expressive fidelity, including motion vigor and posture depth.
Freezing a pre-trained whole-body tracker and learning/distilling an expressiveness-focused residual policy on top is highly practical and effective.
Motion-aware gating, which modulates correction capacity based on reference velocity (activity), prevents unwanted wobble in stationary parts while enabling large, deliberate expressive movements.
Directly incorporating kinetic energy and geometric posture metrics into reward objectives is an effective design principle for expressive humanoid motion generation.
limitations: The five defined descriptors cannot fully capture fine timing discrepancies or whole-body kinetic energy distribution imbalances.
Due to underlying tracker biases and joint limits, trade-offs occur where compensating for one descriptor (e.g., trunk lean) causes unnatural movements in other parts (e.g., legs).
